Learn
LūRN
v. (rendering Hebrew lāmad and Greek manthanō)
From Old English leornian, to get knowledge, related to lāst, a track or footprint — to learn is to follow a trail. The Hebrew lāmad originally means to goad or train, as one trains a heifer to the yoke, and it gives talmīd, a disciple, and the later word Talmud. The Greek manthanō gives mathētēs, a disciple — a learner. The Bible's word for learning is therefore inseparable from its word for discipleship, and both carry the sense of being trained rather than merely informed.

Biblical Definition

Learning in Scripture is practical, personal, and often costly. It is practical because its object is conduct: “Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17) — a list of actions, addressed to a nation whose worship God had just refused. It is personal because its object is finally a Person rather than a subject: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart” (Mat 11:29). The figure is exact — a yoke is what a young beast is trained under, and the Lord offers His own, which is easy, and His burden, which is light, in place of the load the hearer is already carrying. It is costly because some lessons come only through experience: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Php 4:11), written by a man in prison who had known both how to be abased and how to abound, and who says elsewhere that he learned it. And underneath all of it lies the necessity of divine teaching, without which nothing is truly learned at all: “It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me” (Joh 6:45). The learning that ends in Christ is itself the Father's work; there is no coming to the Son except by it.

Webster 1828 Definition

To gain knowledge or skill by instruction, training, or experience; in Scripture inseparable from discipleship, directed to conduct and to the Person of Christ, sometimes taught through affliction, and finally dependent on being taught of God.

expand to see more

LEARN, v.t. 1. To gain knowledge of; to acquire knowledge or ideas of something before unknown.

2. To acquire skill in anything; to gain by practice a faculty of performing.

3. To teach; to communicate the knowledge of something before unknown. This use of the word is now obsolete in good writing, but occurs in the older versions and in common speech.

4. In Scripture, to learn of Christ is to become his disciple, taking his yoke and being trained under it. Matt. 11.

5. To learn by affliction; a frequent Scripture sense. Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now have I kept thy word. Psalm 119. He learned obedience by the things which he suffered. Heb. 5.

Key Scripture

Matthew 11:29 — "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

Isaiah 1:17 — "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."

Philippians 4:11 — "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."

John 6:45 — "It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me."

Modern Corruption

Learning has been separated from obedience and from any master, so that it becomes the accumulation of information by an autonomous mind — the condition Paul describes as ever learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.

expand to see more

The biblical learner is an apprentice under a master, and the biblical test of learning is what he can now do and has now become. Modern learning is largely the acquisition of information by a self-directing mind that submits to no one, and its test is what can be recalled or credentialled. The difference shows most sharply in what each does with a hard saying: the apprentice assumes the fault is his and stays under the yoke; the autonomous learner assumes the fault is the teacher's and moves on. Paul names the end state exactly — ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth — and it is worth noting that he is not describing the ignorant but the perpetually instructed.

There is a matching failure inside the church, where learning is set against doing as though depth of understanding excused delay in obedience. Isaiah writes to people who had the fullest possible liturgical education and whose new moons and appointed feasts God's soul hated; the remedy prescribed is not a further course of instruction but learn to do well, followed by five concrete duties toward the oppressed, the fatherless, and the widow. James says the same in his own idiom: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. The Lord's invitation holds both together and puts them in the right order — take my yoke upon you, and learn of me — the yoke first, and the learning under it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lāmad means to train or goad, and gives talmīd, a disciple. Greek manthanō gives mathētēs, disciple, and appears in the notable wordplay of Heb 5:8, He learned (emathen) obedience by the things which He suffered (epathen).

expand to see more

Hebrew lāmad (H3925) — to learn, to teach, to train; originally of goading cattle. Used in Psa 119:71, that I might learn thy statutes.

Hebrew talmīd (H8527) — a scholar, a disciple; occurring once, in 1Ch 25:8, of those taught in the songs of the LORD.

Greek manthanō (G3129) — to learn, to be instructed, to come to understand by practice; used of learning Christ (Eph 4:20) and learning contentment (Php 4:11).

Greek mathētēs (G3101) — a disciple, a learner; the standard New Testament name for a Christian in the Gospels and Acts, some 268 occurrences.

Greek paideuō (G3811) — to train a child, to instruct, to chastise; the word behind the discipline of Heb 12, in which the Father's correction is itself a form of teaching.

Usage

"Of learning conduct: learn to do well (Isa 1:17); learn first to shew piety at home (1Ti 5:4)."

"Of learning a Person: learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart (Mat 11:29); ye have not so learned Christ (Eph 4:20)."

"Of learning through affliction and of divine teaching: I have learned in whatsoever state I am (Php 4:11); he learned obedience by the things which he suffered (Heb 5:8); they shall be all taught of God (Joh 6:45)."
